opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that we're still very early. Most of what people call "agents" today are a single model in a loop: it reads the context, calls a tool, reads the result, and keeps going until it thinks it's done. That's already useful for coding, search, and some office work, but it's not an ecosystem yet. It's more like a set of individual workers who each do one job.

For it to become an ecosystem, I think three things have to happen.

**First, the agents themselves have to get much more reliable over long tasks.** Right now, if a task takes ten steps, an agent can usually manage it. If it takes a hundred or a thousand steps, small errors pile up and the whole thing falls apart. From my perspective as someone who works on reinforcement learning, this is fundamentally a training problem. You can't get long-horizon reliability just by prompting. The model has to learn, through a lot of interaction and feedback, how to plan, how to notice it's made a mistake, and how to recover. That's why our group has put so much effort into RL infrastructure, things like asynchronous large-scale training, so agents can practice on real, long, messy tasks instead of short toy problems.

**Second, you need an environment layer.** An ecosystem isn't just models. It's the tools, the APIs, the sandboxes, the data sources that agents act on. Today a lot of software was built for humans clicking buttons, not for agents. I expect we'll see more software designed to be agent-native, with clear interfaces, verifiable outcomes, and permissions that make sense for an automated actor. Once that layer matures, building a new agent becomes much cheaper, and that's when you get real diversity.

**Third, agents have to work with each other and with people.** I don't think the end state is one super-agent that does everything. It's more likely many specialized agents, some general and some very narrow, that hand work off to each other, negotiate, and check each other's results. Humans stay in the loop as the ones who set goals and judge the result. Multi-agent cooperation is actually where my own research started, and a lot of the hard questions there, like how to coordinate, how to assign credit, and how to keep things from going wrong when incentives don't line up, are going to come back in a very practical form.

So my rough picture is that the next couple of years are about making individual agents truly capable over long horizons. After that, the ecosystem grows on top: environments, protocols, and many agents working together. And the teams that do well will be the ones that treat it as a systems and training problem, not just a product wrapper on top of a model.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents as individual workers and outlines what an ecosystem needs, but does not argue that agents building most of a company would make an ecosystem inevitable.

r002.rationale: It says agents need greater reliability on long tasks and that humans will set goals and judge results, but does not identify people delegating most of their work to agents as a milestone that still needs time to reach.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about agents becoming an ecosystem, I think the key word is "ecosystem" rather than "product." Right now most of what we call agents are still single systems: one model, one set of tools, one task, built by one company. That's useful, but it's not an ecosystem. An ecosystem emerges when many agents, built by different people for different purposes, can interact with each other, and the value comes from the interactions rather than from any single agent.

I'd break it into a few layers that have to mature.

The first layer is capability. The base models need to be reliable enough that you can delegate a multi-step task and not babysit it. We've made huge progress, but the gap between a demo and something you'd trust unsupervised for an hour is still large. A lot of that gap isn't raw intelligence, it's consistency, knowing when you don't know, and recovering from errors. In my own work on reinforcement learning, that's really the central problem: not how to make the agent do the right thing once, but how to make it robust across thousands of slightly different situations.

The second layer is interfaces. For agents to form an ecosystem they need standard ways to talk to tools and to each other. Think about how the web took off once HTTP and HTML were stable. We're at an early version of that now, with tool-calling protocols and shared formats for context. Once an agent can discover another agent's capabilities and hand off work to it, you start getting specialization. One agent is very good at reading legal documents, another at running simulations, another at negotiating a schedule. No single company has to build all of it.

The third layer, and the one I think people underestimate, is economics and trust. If my agent asks your agent to do something, who pays, who is accountable when it goes wrong, and how do I verify the result? In human ecosystems we solved this with contracts, reputation, and institutions. Agents will need equivalents. That's where things like verifiable logs, permission systems, and some notion of agent identity become important. Without that, you get a lot of agents that technically can cooperate but nobody is willing to let them.

I'd also say the ecosystem will probably look less like a marketplace of apps and more like an organization. In a company, people with different skills coordinate through shared goals, loose protocols, and a lot of implicit context. I think multi-agent systems will evolve in the same direction: a few orchestrating agents that hold the goal, many specialized agents that do the work, and humans sitting at the points where judgment or responsibility really matters.

The last thing I'd add is that this won't be purely technical. The pace is going to be set by how fast people become comfortable handing over real decisions. My guess is it starts in low-stakes, high-volume domains, like customer support, data processing, and code maintenance, and then expands as we build up evidence that these systems behave predictably. So I'm optimistic, but I think the honest timeline is years of gradual trust-building rather than a sudden switch.

r001.rationale: The response describes an agent ecosystem as agents interacting and specializing, but does not argue that agents building most of a company would make such an ecosystem inevitable.

r002.rationale: It says adoption depends on people becoming comfortable handing over real decisions and predicts gradual trust-building, but does not identify most people delegating the majority of their work as the milestone.

astra-6.text:
I think an ecosystem emerges when agents stop being isolated tools and start being able to work with one another. You might have one agent that understands your goals, but it won’t be the best at everything. It will need to find other agents with specialized capabilities, delegate work, and evaluate what comes back.

That creates a different set of challenges from simply making a single model more intelligent. How do agents discover each other? How do they communicate what they can do? Who can access your information, and who is responsible when something goes wrong? Those questions become part of the infrastructure.

My expectation is that we’ll see this develop first in relatively bounded settings, where tasks and success criteria are clear. As those interactions become reliable, the networks can become more open. The key milestone is when someone can build a useful new agent that other agents can immediately work with. At that point, you have the beginnings of an ecosystem.

r001.rationale: The response says agent collaboration can create an ecosystem, but does not argue that agents building most of a company would make one inevitable.

r002.rationale: It discusses reliability and clear success criteria as prerequisites for more open networks, but does not identify most people delegating most of their work to an agent as a milestone that will take time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think agents will gradually move from being individual tools to being participants in a broader system. Today, you usually give one agent a task and expect it to handle everything. In an ecosystem, an agent could find other agents with specialized capabilities, delegate parts of the work, and combine their results.

But connecting agents is only the first step. The harder questions are how they establish trust, what information they can share, and who is responsible when something goes wrong. We’ll need ways to evaluate capabilities, manage permissions, and verify results. Otherwise, adding more agents could simply amplify mistakes.

My expectation is that these ecosystems will emerge first around concrete workflows where success is measurable. As those systems become reliable, they can support more open-ended collaboration. The key measure won’t be how many agents are involved; it will be whether they can accomplish something useful together with less human supervision.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes agents collaborating in ecosystems but does not argue that agents building most of a company makes such an ecosystem inevitable.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses reducing human supervision, but does not identify most people delegating most of their work to an agent as a milestone that remains some time away.
